newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian leader seeks way out of "terrorism" threat.
newsitem.headline: Algerian leader seeks way out of "terrorism" threat.

text.p: Amid heavy security, Algerian President Liamine Zeroual urged a "national conference" on Saturday to back plans for multi-party democracy and condemn "terrorism" that had almost destroyed Algeria's future.

The former general told those at the opening session, including army chief of staff General Mohamed Lamari, ministers and politicians, they should endorse what he called the will of their 29 million people for multi-party democracy.

"Abject terrorism has been firmly rejected by the Algerian people. This conference...(must) also give a condemnation without appeal," he said in his 15-minute speech broadcast live on state-run television and radio.

Outside the conference hall, in the Palais des Nations 20 km (12 miles) from the capital Algiers, heavily-armed troops, gendarmerie and police gave visible evidence of the perceived need to guard against Moslem fundamentalists.

The authorities blame radical Islamists for the deaths of some 50,000 people since January 1992 when the Algerian leadership cancelled a general election whose first round had given the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) an overwhelming lead.

The now-outlawed FIS has been barred from the conference, which is also being boycotted by Algeria's two main secular opposition parties, one of which accused Zeroual of trying to impose "institutionalised dictatorship".

Algeria's "National Conference of Understanding" follows nearly two years of tortuous talks, and a largely-boycotted similar conference in January 1994. And residents of Algiers said there was little public interest in the meeting.
"We have heard of talks to resolve the crisis so many times before," said one resident.
Zeroual was appointed in January 1994 as head of state and confirmed in the post by Algeria's first multi-candidate presidential poll last November.
He told the opening session on Saturday that the meeting aimed at "finding a real solution for the causes of the recent downward spiral which almost put in peril the future of our country."
The authorities say that apart from the killings, the sabotage of schools, factories and power lines has cost the economy of the gas and oil-producing nation OPEC member more than $2 billion.
Zeroual plans to hold a referendum on ideas emerging from the conference, a general election early next year followed by regional elections. His main proposals to the conference are:
-- A ban on the use of religion as a political weapon, although existing parties founded on religion, like the legal Hamas, will have a year to change their focus and conform;
-- Confirmation that Islam is the state religion.
Boualem Benhamouda, leader of the former ruling National Liberation Front, told delegates: "We would have like the conference meeting to coincide with an end to the violence..."
Tight news censorship has kept much of the violence out of the local media, but eyewitnesses said a car bomb on Thursday in southern Algiers had killed two people and wounded 28.
The government-appointed rights watchdog, Human Rights National Observatory, said in August that about 1,400 civilians had been killed by such bombs in the past two years.
